Photo: Ayọ̀ Akínwándé.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Self’s practice has long used bodily distortion and exaggeration. Breasts expand. Hips widen. Buttocks become enormous. Bodies are constructed and reconstructed through paint, fabric, print and collage. Self knows the visual history into which these figures enter. She has spoken about the iconographic significance of the Black female body, the fantasies projected onto it, and reclaiming physical characteristics historically turned into objects of fetish and ridicule."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Kara Walker and Thomas J Price offer two useful counterpoints. Walker’s monumental A Subtlety (2014), installed inside Brooklyn’s former Domino Sugar Refinery, deliberately mobilised the mammy and the hypersexualised Black female body. The stereotype was not incidental to the work; it was part of the history Walker was forcing into view. Price takes another route. His Grounded in the Stars (2023), a twelve-foot bronze installed in Times Square in 2025, monumentalised an anonymous, large-bodied Black woman in everyday clothes. The work’s ordinariness is precisely the point: her body does not need to become heroic, exceptional or conventionally idealised to deserve monumental scale. These examples clarify what troubles me about Self. The problem is not that Lady in Blue is large, Black or female. It is whether a visual language historically entangled with the stereotyping of Black female bodies can simultaneously sustain Self’s claim to the “everywoman.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The exaggeration is not accidental, nor is its history. The Black female body has spent centuries being made spectacular within the Western imagination. From the exhibition and exploitation of Sarah Baartman in nineteenth-century Europe to recurring fixations on Black women’s breasts, buttocks and sexuality in contemporary popular culture, bodily exaggeration has rarely been innocent. Hip hop, advertising, pornography and social media did not invent this vocabulary. They inherited and transformed it."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Self’s practice approaches that history through reclamation and self-determination. Speaking about her sustained engagement with the Black female body, she has said, “It’s the body I feel I can have the most honest conversation about because it’s my own.” Her position matters here: the body is not simply an image inherited from someone else’s gaze, but a subject through which she asserts her own intentions and aspirations."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I understand that position. But what troubles me is what happens when that strategy leaves the studio and gallery, becomes more than five metres tall and is elevated above one of Britain’s most symbolically charged public squares as an everywoman."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Trafalgar Square is not a neutral exhibition surface. It is an architectural composition of power and memory. King George IV surveys the square from his column while statues of Sir Charles James Napier and Sir Henry Havelock occupy its other plinth. The Fourth Plinth was left unresolved by that monumental scheme and has subsequently become a place where contemporary art interrupts it. Every work installed there enters into conversation with the architecture, the imperial histories around it and the thousands of bodies moving through the square below."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Scale changes an image, elevation changes it, and so does site. This is where Eisenman’s distinction keeps returning to me."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Public sculpture does not wait for us to enter it. We do not buy a ticket or choose the exhibition. It occupies our routes through the city and becomes part of the visual environment of people who may know nothing about the artist or her intentions. What if precisely this body had been designed by a white British male sculptor? What if he had exaggerated the breasts, hips and buttocks of a Black woman, put her in platform shoes and a blue dress, enlarged her to monumental scale and presented her as an everyday woman? Would we be as generous in our reading?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Authorship matters. History makes it impossible to pretend that a Black woman representing a Black female body and a white man doing so are equivalent acts. But authorship cannot become the end of looking. The blue emerges from the uniform associated with Black domestic workers in South Africa, a history intimately connected to Sibande’s family. Her mother, grandmother and great-grandmother worked as domestic workers. Mary Sibande, Sophie-Elsie , 2009. Life-size fibreglass figure, cotton textile, nylon, plastic button detailing and foam padding. 183 x 200 x 175 cm. Image courtesy of the artist."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Sophie-Elsie-1-1-1030x772.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "Mary Sibande, Sophie-Elsie , 2009. Life-size fibreglass figure, cotton textile, nylon, plastic button detailing and foam padding. 183 x 200 x 175 cm. Image courtesy of the artist.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Sibande allows the uniform of service to mutate. Sophie becomes aristocratic, excessive, impossible. She dreams herself beyond the position apartheid prepared for her. Mary Sibande’s blue remembers. Mary Sibande, Sophie-Elsie , 2009. Life-size fibreglass figure, cotton textile, nylon, plastic button detailing and foam padding. 183 x 200 x 175 cm. Image courtesy of the artist."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Sophie-Elsie-2-1030x1030.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "Mary Sibande, Sophie-Elsie , 2009. Life-size fibreglass figure, cotton textile, nylon, plastic button detailing and foam padding. 183 x 200 x 175 cm. Image courtesy of the artist.", "credit": "ART AFRICA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Self’s blue remembers something different. Lapis lazuli, the stone from which natural ultramarine was historically extracted, travelled from mines in Afghanistan into European painting, where its rarity and cost made blue a material of value as much as colour. It became particularly associated with the robes of the Virgin Mary. In Lady in Blue , that chromatic history of preciousness and elevation is transferred to a woman Self insists is not an idol or historic figure, but an everyday person. But standing in London, I cannot help asking what else the blue might have remembered."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Britain possesses its own vast archive of Black womanhood. Caribbean women arrived in postwar Britain and became nurses, midwives, cleaners and carers in the National Health Service. There are the women of the Windrush generation and their descendants. There are Black women in universities, corporations, hospitals, media, law, schools, government and the arts. There are women of African and Caribbean heritage whose histories cannot be compressed into a single Black British experience."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I initially wondered whether the woman on the plinth should have been one of those NHS women. There is something powerful about monumentalising the Black woman whose everyday labour has literally kept British people alive."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But that creates another problem. Why must the Black woman serve Britain before Britain permits her to become monumental? Why must she nurse, clean, migrate, struggle, mother or overcome something before she earns the pedestal?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Self is right to resist that demand. A Black woman should be able simply to exist in a blue dress, walking somewhere, without justifying her presence through sacrifice. The problem is not that Self failed to sculpt a nurse; it is the enormous representational burden contained in the word “everywoman.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Britain already possesses a small but revealing history of Black female figuration in public sculpture. Bronze Woman (2008), conceived through Cécile Nobrega’s poem and campaign, carries histories of Caribbean migration and motherhood. Martin Jennings’s Mary Seacole (2016) stands outside St Thomas’ Hospital. Thomas J Price’s Reaching Out (2020) gives us an anonymous contemporary Black woman absorbed in her phone. Basil Watson’s National Windrush Monument (2022) places a woman within an intergenerational migrant family. Veronica Ryan avoids representing the Black body altogether in Custard Apple (Annonaceae) , Breadfruit (Moraceae) and Soursop (Annonaceae) (2021), allowing objects to carry histories of Caribbean migration and memory."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Fourth Plinth itself offers another precedent. In 2003, Nigerian-born British sculptor Sokari Douglas Camp was shortlisted with No-o War-r No-o-War-r (2003), a group of stainless-steel protesters carrying antiwar placards in response to demonstrations that had occupied Trafalgar Square. She allowed the site’s recent history to enter the proposed sculpture."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I find myself wondering what would have happened if the plinth had refused singularity altogether. Imagine moving around it and encountering not the Black woman but Black women. Different ages, bodies and relationships to London. One might work in the city, another in the NHS, academia or the arts. Perhaps none of those professions needs to be announced. The point is not to produce a checklist of respectable Black achievement; it is to refuse the expectation that one body can carry everybody else."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I am not proposing this as the sculpture Self should have made. Artists do not owe critics the artworks we would prefer them to produce. I imagine these multiple women only to expose the contradiction within the idea of a singular Black “everywoman”: the moment one body is asked to stand for everyone, all the differences that make such universality impossible begin to appear."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "There is a cruel irony here. Racist spectators look at Lady in Blue and find an opportunity to ridicule a Black body. Celebratory spectators see representation, confidence and progress. article_text:
In this critical reflection for ART AFRICA, Ayọ̀ Akínwándé examines Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue (2026), installed on Trafalgar Square’s Fourth Plinth, and questions the histories, stereotypes, and expectations carried by the monumental Black female body. Beginning with a conversation between Nicole Eisenman and curator Mark Godfrey, Akínwándé considers how authorship, artistic intention, and public space shape representation, and whether celebrating Black visibility has made its images harder to question. At its centre is a provocative proposition: can one Black woman ever be expected to represent the universal “everywoman”?

Ayọ̀ Akínwándé

On 29 September 2026, I sat in the Royal Institution in London listening to Nicole Eisenman in conversation with curator Mark Godfrey. The conversation centred, in part, on Eisenman’s monumental sculpture Stack (2022), recently installed in the courtyard of the Royal Academy of Arts.

Standing more than eight metres high, Stack rises through a precarious accumulation of figures and objects. An artist carries a wine barrel. Above it sits a giant potato, then Eisenman’s cat, Edie. At the summit, the late British sculptor Phyllida Barlow balances a vase of flowers on her head. Nicole Eisenman Stack , 2022 Sculpture, Royal Academy of Arts, London ©Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth. Photo: Ayọ̀ Akínwándé.

During the conversation, Eisenman traced Stack to an earlier painting, Hindsight (2020), which appeared on the screen behind her. The architecture of accumulation was already there, but the figure occupying its upper reaches was different: a large, pale, naked figure, turned away from the viewer. During the question-and-answer session, a member of the audience asked whether the figure was intended to be Donald Trump. As I recall the exchange, Eisenman responded that it was not Trump, but simply a fat white man. I am paraphrasing the exchange from memory rather than quoting either speaker verbatim. Nicole Eisenman, Hindsight , 2020, Oil on canvas, 208.6 x 165.7 cm / 82 1/8 x 65 1/4 inches © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth. Photo: Thomas Barratt.

What interested me was not whether the man was Trump. It was why he disappeared.

As I understood Eisenman’s explanation that evening, painting offered a different kind of privacy. A painting could be made within the privacy of the studio and might eventually enter another private space, including someone’s home. Sculpture entering the public realm demanded another kind of consideration. My recollection is that Eisenman described becoming more intentional about the figure that would occupy that public space.

The anonymous man did not make that journey. Phyllida Barlow did. Barlow, who died in 2023, had been Eisenman’s friend, mentor and an important influence on her understanding of sculpture. Eisenman also spoke about allowing time after Barlow’s death before publicly presenting the work, so that the gesture could properly honour her. Members of Barlow’s family were in the room that evening. Nicole Eisenman, Hindsight , 2020, Oil on canvas, 208.6 x 165.7 cm / 82 1/8 x 65 1/4 inches © Nicole Eisenman. Courtesy of the artist and Hauser & Wirth. Photo: Thomas Barratt.

What stayed with me was the distinction Eisenman drew between making an image privately and placing a body publicly. And that who we put into public space matters. I left the Royal Institution thinking again about another monumental woman standing less than two miles away.

Tschabalala Self’s Lady in Blue (2026) has occupied the Fourth Plinth in Trafalgar Square since 10 September. More than five metres high, she is cast in bronze, dressed in intense blue, adorned with jewellery and platform shoes, and caught mid-stride as though she has somewhere to be. Tschabalala Self, Lady in Blue , 2026. Painted bronze sculpture. Fourth Plinth, Trafalgar Square, London. Commissioned through the Mayor of London’s Fourth Plinth programme. Photo: Ayọ̀ Akínwándé.

I had been thinking about her before Eisenman’s conversation. More accurately, I had been disturbed by her. Listening to Eisenman helped me understand why.

Self is a Black American woman who has achieved one of the most visible public art commissions in the world. Her sculpture also enters a public sphere in which images of Black people continue to attract racist hostility. Self knows this intimately. Her earlier public sculpture Seated (2022) was vandalised at the De La Warr Pavilion.

Since Lady in Blue appeared in Trafalgar Square, I have watched some reactions online descend quickly into racist caricature. The Black female body remains extraordinarily available for public ridicule. Perhaps that is precisely why criticism becomes difficult. But representation cannot mean suspending criticism.

Self has been explicit about the figure she intended to place in Trafalgar Square. At the unveiling, she described Lady in Blue as “an everyday person much like the many who occupy the square daily,” adding that the figure is “striding forward into our collective future with ambition, purpose and optimism.” The Fourth Plinth programme itself describes the commission as an attempt to bring a contemporary “everywoman” to the square. I take that proposition seriously. Self is asking this anonymous Black woman to operate not simply as a representation of Black womanhood, but as an everyday figure with a claim to universality.

It is a compelling question. But another sits beside it. What kind of Black woman have we chosen to make universal? Tschabalala Self, Lady in Blue , 2026. Painted bronze sculpture. Fourth Plinth, Trafalgar Square, London. Commissioned through the Mayor of London’s Fourth Plinth programme. Photo: Ayọ̀ Akínwándé.

Self’s practice has long used bodily distortion and exaggeration. Breasts expand. Hips widen. Buttocks become enormous. Bodies are constructed and reconstructed through paint, fabric, print and collage. Self knows the visual history into which these figures enter. She has spoken about the iconographic significance of the Black female body, the fantasies projected onto it, and reclaiming physical characteristics historically turned into objects of fetish and ridicule.

Kara Walker and Thomas J Price offer two useful counterpoints. Walker’s monumental A Subtlety (2014), installed inside Brooklyn’s former Domino Sugar Refinery, deliberately mobilised the mammy and the hypersexualised Black female body. The stereotype was not incidental to the work; it was part of the history Walker was forcing into view. Price takes another route. His Grounded in the Stars (2023), a twelve-foot bronze installed in Times Square in 2025, monumentalised an anonymous, large-bodied Black woman in everyday clothes. The work’s ordinariness is precisely the point: her body does not need to become heroic, exceptional or conventionally idealised to deserve monumental scale. These examples clarify what troubles me about Self. The problem is not that Lady in Blue is large, Black or female. It is whether a visual language historically entangled with the stereotyping of Black female bodies can simultaneously sustain Self’s claim to the “everywoman.”

The exaggeration is not accidental, nor is its history. The Black female body has spent centuries being made spectacular within the Western imagination. From the exhibition and exploitation of Sarah Baartman in nineteenth-century Europe to recurring fixations on Black women’s breasts, buttocks and sexuality in contemporary popular culture, bodily exaggeration has rarely been innocent. Hip hop, advertising, pornography and social media did not invent this vocabulary. They inherited and transformed it.

Self’s practice approaches that history through reclamation and self-determination. Speaking about her sustained engagement with the Black female body, she has said, “It’s the body I feel I can have the most honest conversation about because it’s my own.” Her position matters here: the body is not simply an image inherited from someone else’s gaze, but a subject through which she asserts her own intentions and aspirations.

I understand that position. But what troubles me is what happens when that strategy leaves the studio and gallery, becomes more than five metres tall and is elevated above one of Britain’s most symbolically charged public squares as an everywoman.

Trafalgar Square is not a neutral exhibition surface. It is an architectural composition of power and memory. King George IV surveys the square from his column while statues of Sir Charles James Napier and Sir Henry Havelock occupy its other plinth. The Fourth Plinth was left unresolved by that monumental scheme and has subsequently become a place where contemporary art interrupts it. Every work installed there enters into conversation with the architecture, the imperial histories around it and the thousands of bodies moving through the square below.

Scale changes an image, elevation changes it, and so does site. This is where Eisenman’s distinction keeps returning to me.

Public sculpture does not wait for us to enter it. We do not buy a ticket or choose the exhibition. It occupies our routes through the city and becomes part of the visual environment of people who may know nothing about the artist or her intentions. If the audience changes, surely the conditions of representation change with it.

I keep returning to an uncomfortable thought experiment. What if precisely this body had been designed by a white British male sculptor? What if he had exaggerated the breasts, hips and buttocks of a Black woman, put her in platform shoes and a blue dress, enlarged her to monumental scale and presented her as an everyday woman? Would we be as generous in our reading?

Authorship matters. History makes it impossible to pretend that a Black woman representing a Black female body and a white man doing so are equivalent acts. But authorship cannot become the end of looking. Otherwise, identity begins to operate as an exemption from criticism.

I think of another woman in blue when I look at Self’s sculpture. In Sophie/Elsie (2009), South African artist Mary Sibande casts her alter ego Sophie from her own body and envelops her in a spectacular blue Victorian dress. The blue emerges from the uniform associated with Black domestic workers in South Africa, a history intimately connected to Sibande’s family. Her mother, grandmother and great-grandmother worked as domestic workers. Mary Sibande, Sophie-Elsie , 2009. Life-size fibreglass figure, cotton textile, nylon, plastic button detailing and foam padding. 183 x 200 x 175 cm. Image courtesy of the artist.

Sibande allows the uniform of service to mutate. Sophie becomes aristocratic, excessive, impossible. She dreams herself beyond the position apartheid prepared for her. Mary Sibande’s blue remembers. Mary Sibande, Sophie-Elsie , 2009. Life-size fibreglass figure, cotton textile, nylon, plastic button detailing and foam padding. 183 x 200 x 175 cm. Image courtesy of the artist.

Self’s blue remembers something different. Lapis lazuli, the stone from which natural ultramarine was historically extracted, travelled from mines in Afghanistan into European painting, where its rarity and cost made blue a material of value as much as colour. It became particularly associated with the robes of the Virgin Mary. In Lady in Blue , that chromatic history of preciousness and elevation is transferred to a woman Self insists is not an idol or historic figure, but an everyday person. But standing in London, I cannot help asking what else the blue might have remembered.

Britain possesses its own vast archive of Black womanhood. Caribbean women arrived in postwar Britain and became nurses, midwives, cleaners and carers in the National Health Service. There are the women of the Windrush generation and their descendants. There are Black women in universities, corporations, hospitals, media, law, schools, government and the arts. There are women of African and Caribbean heritage whose histories cannot be compressed into a single Black British experience.

I initially wondered whether the woman on the plinth should have been one of those NHS women. There is something powerful about monumentalising the Black woman whose everyday labour has literally kept British people alive.

But that creates another problem. Why must the Black woman serve Britain before Britain permits her to become monumental? Why must she nurse, clean, migrate, struggle, mother or overcome something before she earns the pedestal?

Self is right to resist that demand. A Black woman should be able simply to exist in a blue dress, walking somewhere, without justifying her presence through sacrifice. The problem is not that Self failed to sculpt a nurse; it is the enormous representational burden contained in the word “everywoman.”

Britain already possesses a small but revealing history of Black female figuration in public sculpture. Bronze Woman (2008), conceived through Cécile Nobrega’s poem and campaign, carries histories of Caribbean migration and motherhood. Martin Jennings’s Mary Seacole (2016) stands outside St Thomas’ Hospital. Thomas J Price’s Reaching Out (2020) gives us an anonymous contemporary Black woman absorbed in her phone. Basil Watson’s National Windrush Monument (2022) places a woman within an intergenerational migrant family. Veronica Ryan avoids representing the Black body altogether in Custard Apple (Annonaceae) , Breadfruit (Moraceae) and Soursop (Annonaceae) (2021), allowing objects to carry histories of Caribbean migration and memory.

The Fourth Plinth itself offers another precedent. In 2003, Nigerian-born British sculptor Sokari Douglas Camp was shortlisted with No-o War-r No-o-War-r (2003), a group of stainless-steel protesters carrying antiwar placards in response to demonstrations that had occupied Trafalgar Square. She allowed the site’s recent history to enter the proposed sculpture.

I find myself wondering what would have happened if the plinth had refused singularity altogether. Imagine moving around it and encountering not the Black woman but Black women. Different ages, bodies and relationships to London. One might work in the city, another in the NHS, academia or the arts. Perhaps none of those professions needs to be announced. The point is not to produce a checklist of respectable Black achievement; it is to refuse the expectation that one body can carry everybody else.

I am not proposing this as the sculpture Self should have made. Artists do not owe critics the artworks we would prefer them to produce. I imagine these multiple women only to expose the contradiction within the idea of a singular Black “everywoman”: the moment one body is asked to stand for everyone, all the differences that make such universality impossible begin to appear.

There is a cruel irony here. Racist spectators look at Lady in Blue and find an opportunity to ridicule a Black body. Celebratory spectators see representation, confidence and progress. Both responses can prevent us from asking a harder question about the image itself. Perhaps representation matures when we are capable of doing something other than celebrating its arrival.

There is an African proverb frequently associated with Chinua Achebe’s thinking about history: “Until the lions have their own historians, the history of the hunt will always glorify the hunter.” Its force lies in authorship. The hunter does not only possess the weapon; he possesses the story. He decides how the hunt is remembered, who becomes heroic, and who remains merely the hunted. Who has been permitted to describe whom? Who controls the archive? Who produces the image?

For centuries, Black people have demanded the right to become authors of our own images. Contemporary culture is full of the language of finally being able to “tell our own stories,” and “speak our truth.” These are important gains. But authorship does not happen outside systems of power. The question is not only who gets to tell the story, but which stories institutions choose to commission, elevate and validate. Visibility, after all, is not the same as agency: being seen does not necessarily mean determining the conditions under which one becomes visible.

What happens, then, when the lion finally becomes the historian, but the conditions under which the story becomes visible are still shaped by the institutions that once privileged the hunter? Surely the answer cannot be that the lion’s account is beyond criticism.

Tschabalala Self has every right to put this woman into Trafalgar Square. She has every right to exaggerate her, reclaim her, dress her in blue and insist that she stands not simply for Black womanhood but for humanity. And those of us looking at her have an equal right to ask what histories arrived on the plinth with her.

Perhaps the wrong Black woman has been put on the Fourth Plinth.

Not because somewhere in Britain there is a more respectable Black woman waiting for the pedestal. Not because the woman standing there is insufficiently British, modest, heroic or accomplished.

Perhaps she is wrong because the expectation that one Black woman can become the Black everywoman was wrong in the first place. And perhaps the most meaningful consequence of finally getting the opportunity to tell the story of the hunt is not that we all agree on the story. It is that, at last, we can argue about it.

Ayọ̀ Akínwándé is a British-Nigerian artist working across painting, lens-based media, installation, sound, and performance. His work examines power, socio-political realities, and the interplay of tradition and modernity. He is also a curator, researcher, and writer, with international exhibitions and curatorial projects, including co-curating the inaugural Lagos Biennial (2017).

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: After a decade-long effort to secure the film rights to I Never Promised You a Rose Garden — Joanne Greenberg ’s classic 1964 novel, which she calls “one of the most arresting and authentic explorations of mental illness ever written” — Ashley Avis has done it.

The rising filmmaker, whose credits include Disney+’s Black Beauty , will direct from her own script and produce alongside Edward Winters through her Winterstone Pictures banner.

Inspired by Greenberg’s experiences as a young woman diagnosed with schizophrenia, I Never Promised You a Rose Garden follows Deborah Blau, a brilliant and deeply troubled Jewish teenager who retreats into an elaborate kingdom she has constructed within her own mind.

Related Stories

From 'Black Beauty' To 'Wild Beauty': Director Ashley Avis' Equine Activism Comes Full Circle In Her Oscar-Contending Documentary

Sugar23 Signs 'Wild Beauty' Filmmaker Ashley Avis

As Deborah loses her grip on reality, she’s admitted to Chestnut Lodge, where she forms an unlikely bond with renowned German psychiatrist Dr. Clara Fried, whose own past remains shrouded in unresolved trauma and mystery. In the years following World War II, these two women must navigate the fragile boundary between reality and fantasy, forging a unique relationship that challenges the fabric of mental health as we know it.

Watch on Deadline

Regarded as a seminal work on mental health, I Never Promised You a Rose Garden has sold millions of copies worldwide and previously inspired an Academy Award-nominated 1977 film, directed by Anthony Page and starring Kathleen Quinlan.

Avis told us of the novel, “Joanne Greenberg crafted a story that is at once deeply intimate and breathtakingly imaginative, because it is courageously personal. She invites us into the Kingdom of Yr, into all of its seduction, and beauty along with its violence – and we will question, along with Deborah, whether it is possible to give it up.”

What moved Avis most about the book “was the true story tucked between the pages of Rose Garden; the relationship between two very real women who inspired these characters. Deborah Blau and Dr. Fried become mirrors for one another as they navigate darkness, trauma, healing, and the question of what it means to truly live in, and accept, reality.”

A great lover of animals — and horses, in particular — Avis channeled that passion into the two films for which she’s best known: a Disney+ adaptation of Anna Sewell’s classic 1877 novel Black Beauty , starring Kate Winslet and Mackenzie Foy, and the Critics Choice Award-nominated documentary Wild Beauty: Mustang Spirit of the West . Currently, Avis is developing American Wolf — a film on the wolves of Yellowstone, based on the novel by Nate Blakeslee — with Appian Way. Additionally, she has set up a reimagining of Wim Wenders’ romance City of Angels at Warner Bros. She is represented by CAA and Ryan Goodell of Yorn, Levine, Barnes.

article_text:
1976年刊行の絵本「はじめてのおつかい」は今も読み継がれている名作。絵を手がけた林明子さんは子どもたちの生き生きとした姿を描き続けてきました。アニメーション映画監督の宮崎駿さんも魅了したその描写の秘密を、俳優の蓮佛美沙子が原画やラフスケッチを鑑賞し紐解いていきます。さらにアトリエに残されていたのは、人物を撮影した膨大な量の写真。その目的は？

目指したのは現実の世界よりも本物に感じられる世界！この絵本をはじめ数々の名作を残した絵本作家の真実に迫ります。

（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班）

title_original: How Keanu Reeves Landed in Stop-Motion Samurai Epic ‘Hidari’ – and Why S.S. Rajamouli Wanted to Know How It Was Made
editorial_title_zh: 基努·里维斯如何加盟定格动画武士史诗《Hidari》——以及S·S·拉贾穆里为何想知道它是怎么拍出来的
editorial_excerpt_zh: 导演川村真人（Kawamura Masashi）在东京国际电影节上表示，基努·里维斯在观看了该项目的试播片后决定加盟日本定格动画长片《Hidari》，安排放映大约一周后，他的团队便与电影制作人取得联系并安排了一场Zoom通话……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "导演川村真人在东京国际电影节上表示，基努·里维斯在观看了日本定格动画长片《Hidari》的试播片后便决定加入该项目，安排放映大约一周后，他的团队便与电影制作人取得联系并安排了一场Zoom通话。他在电影节上还更新了该片的资金筹集进展。", "links": [{"text": "Keanu Reeves", "url": "https://variety.com/t/keanu-reeves/"}, {"text": "Hidari", "url": "https://variety.com/t/hidari/"}, {"text": "Tokyo International Film Festival", "url": "https://variety.com/t/tokyo-international-film-festival/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为《Hidari》的创作者、编剧兼导演，川村与联合导演小川育一同出席了一场关于“电影前沿”（Film Frontier）项目的成果汇报会。该人才发展项目由日本文化厅资助、电影节主办方UniJapan运营，此前已为该团队前往各大电影市场和行业活动的差旅提供了资金支持。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "相关报道", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/amanda-2.jpg?w=250&h=167&crop=1", "alt": "德国柏林 - 2月19日：阿曼达·塞弗里德（Amanda Seyfried）于2026年2月19日在德国柏林君悦酒店举办的第76届柏林国际电影节《安·李的遗嘱》（The Testament Of Ann Lee）拍照环节上摆姿势留影。（图片来源：Arturo Holmes/Getty Images）", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "阿曼达·塞弗里德拒绝激情戏并曾拒绝一部“我必须一直发生性关系”的电视剧：我不想“和一个陌生人赤诚相见”", "links": [{"text": "Amanda Seyfried Rejects Sex Scenes and Turned Down a TV Series Where 'I'd Have to Have Sex All the Time': I Don't Want to Be 'Naked With a Stranger'", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/film/news/amanda-seyfried-bans-sex-scenes-1236908927/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://variety.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/You-Can-See-everything.jpg?w=250&h=167&crop=1", "alt": "内森·菲尔德（Nathan Fielder）在《你可以看到一切》（You Can See Everything）中", "caption": "", "credit": "Variety · Film", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "《你可以看到一切》：伊丽莎白·霍姆斯（Elizabeth Holmes）纪录片中那个震撼的元叙事反转[剧透]解析", "links": [{"text": "'You Can See Everything': That Shocking, Meta Twist With [SPOILER] Explained in Elizabeth Holmes Doc", "url": "https://variety.com/2026/film/news/you-can-see-everything-amanda-seyfried-elizabeth-holmes-1236914390/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "里维斯将为主角配音的消息于5月在戛纳电影节上公布，不过川村表示，这位演员在电影节之前就已经看过了试播片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "川村说：“我们深受黑泽明电影的影响，所以在制作偶人时，我要求把三船敏郎和基努·里维斯加在一起、二等分，再加上岁月的痕迹。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "自那以后，川村一直将里维斯列为主角配音的首选。该片的制片人对此十分认真，设法联系上了这位演员并安排他观看了试播片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "川村说：“大约一周后我们收到了回复，对方说：‘行，我们连线个Zoom吧。’当时我在想，现在事情进展得这么快。然后我们接通了电话，基努就坐在屏幕的那头。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Hidari》也吸引了《RRR》导演S·S·拉贾穆里的目光。川村说，他是在安讷西见到这位印度导演的，并向他展示了《Hidari》，两人最后站着聊了大约30分钟，讨论这部电影是如何制作出来的。", "links": [{"text": "S.S. Rajamouli", "url": "https://variety.com/t/s-s-rajamouli/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "川村说：“他说：‘你们太厉害了。这是怎么做出来的？’”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "川村表示，像这样与平时难得有机会交集的导演偶遇，只有在电影节上才会发生。他说：“影厅里有惊喜，走出影厅后则有各种连接。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "据川村介绍，该团队大约在三年前拍摄了这个概念验证短片，靠自筹资金并在众筹的帮助下完成，并将其发布到了YouTube上。自那以后，它已经获得了约530万次观看和大约12万名关注者，其中许多来自海外。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他说：“木雕、定格动画再加上时代剧——这是一个非常简朴的项目。如果我们仅凭一份文字提案去推介，我想没有人能理解它。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在“电影前沿”的支持下，电影人携带着其中一个手雕偶人，在戛纳电影市场旗下的安讷西动画展示会上推介了《Hidari》。川村表示，这个偶人吸引的围观群众比它的创作者还要多，而戛纳这个平台让这部电影走进了真人片和动作片影迷、发行商以及经纪人的视野。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "川村说：“定格动画是一个很小的圈子，人们往往会觉得它是一个狭窄的市场。但尽管它是定格动画，我们在构思时也是把它当作一部动作片来对待的。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "川村表示，该片的预算庞大，团队目前仍在推销该项目、寻求海外发行商的资助与合作。他补充道：“从节奏上讲，我们是以独立电影的方式在制作它。多亏了我们行动敏捷，这个项目才得以踩着薄冰坚持到现在。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "本月早些时候在釜山，Dwarf Studios的制片人松本纪子（Matsumoto Noriko）表示，他们曾与一家美国公司进行过洽谈，对方提出出资包揽全部预算以换取全部版权，但目前谈判已经陷入停滞。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在定格动画公司Dwarf Studios工作的小川今年出席了安讷西动画节。他表示，在商业电影和电视动画中，这种技术依然属于小众，但电影节短片和学生单元里到处都是它的身影，来自欧洲、北美及其他地区的动画工作室纷纷汇聚安讷西。他说：“当我把这个偶人带去时，它大受欢迎。这真的很有趣。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "已步入第三个年头的“电影前沿”项目是文化厅创作者支援基金的一部分，该基金为创作者提供大约三年的支持，涵盖从项目开发到海外推广的全过程。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Keanu Reeves joined Japanese stop-motion feature “ Hidari ” after watching the project’s pilot film, with his team getting back to the filmmakers about a week after the screening was arranged to set up a Zoom call, director Kawamura Masashi said at the Tokyo International Film Festival , where he also updated the film’s fundraising push.

Kawamura, who created, wrote and is directing “Hidari,” appeared with co-director Ogawa Iku at a session reporting on Film Frontier, a talent development program backed by Japan’s Agency for Cultural Affairs and run by festival organizer UniJapan. The program has paid for the team’s travel to markets and industry events.

Related Stories

Amanda Seyfried Rejects Sex Scenes and Turned Down a TV Series Where 'I'd Have to Have Sex All the Time': I Don't Want to Be 'Naked With a Stranger'

'You Can See Everything': That Shocking, Meta Twist With [SPOILER] Explained in Elizabeth Holmes Doc

Reeves’ casting as the lead voice was announced at Cannes in May, but Kawamura said the actor had seen the pilot before the festival.

“We were heavily influenced by Kurosawa’s films, so when the puppet was being made, I asked for Mifune Toshiro and Keanu Reeves added together, divided by two and then aged,” Kawamura said.

From then on, Kawamura kept Reeves at the top of his list for the lead voice. The film’s producers took that seriously, found a way to reach the actor and arranged for him to watch the pilot.

“About a week later we heard back, and it was, ‘OK, let’s do a Zoom,’” Kawamura said. “I was thinking, so this is how fast things move these days. Then we got on the call and Keanu was there on the other side.”

“Hidari” has also caught the eye of “RRR” director S.S. Rajamouli . Kawamura said he met the Indian filmmaker at Annecy, showed him “Hidari” and ended up in a standing conversation of about 30 minutes about how the film was made.

“He said, ‘You’re amazing. How did you make this?’” Kawamura said.

Kawamura said an encounter like that, with a director he would rarely cross paths with otherwise, could only happen at a festival. “There’s the surprise inside the theater, and there are the connections after you walk out,” he said.

The team shot the proof-of-concept short around three years ago, paying for it themselves with help from crowdfunding, and posted it on YouTube. It has since drawn about 5.3 million views and roughly 120,000 followers, many of them overseas, according to Kawamura.

“Wood carving, stop-motion and a period drama – it’s a very austere project,” he said. “If we’d pitched it with just a written proposal, I don’t think anyone would have understood it.”

With Film Frontier support, the filmmakers pitched “Hidari” at the Annecy Animation Showcase, part of the Cannes Film Market, carrying one of the hand-carved puppets with them. Kawamura said the puppet drew bigger crowds than its makers, and the Cannes platform put the film in front of live-action and action fans as well as distributors and agents.

“Stop-motion is a really small world, and people tend to assume it’s a narrow market,” Kawamura said. “But even though it’s stop-motion, we think of it as an action film.”

The budget is large, and the team is still out selling the project, seeking grants and partnerships with overseas distributors, Kawamura said. “In terms of speed, we’re making it the indie way,” he added. “Thanks to being light on our feet, I think the project has managed to make it across thin ice.”

Earlier this month in Busan, Dwarf Studios producer Matsumoto Noriko said talks with a U.S. company that had offered to fund the entire budget, in exchange for all the rights, had stalled.

Ogawa, who works at stop-motion house Dwarf Studios, attended Annecy this year. He said the technique remains niche in commercial film and TV animation, but festival shorts and student sections are full of it, and studios from Europe, North America and beyond converge on Annecy. “When I took the puppet along, it was hugely popular,” he said. “It was fun.”

Film Frontier, now in its third year, is part of the Agency for Cultural Affairs’ Creator Support Fund, which backs creators for around three years, from project development through to overseas rollout.

title_original: Historian Lucy Worsley looks back: ‘The story of my life has been – the bookworm shall go to the ball’
editorial_title_zh: 历史学家露西·沃斯利回首往事：“我的人生故事就是——书呆子终将去参加舞会”
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这位节目主持人回忆了自己曾是个“怪异的小书呆子”、差一点成为科学家，以及她在工作中穿过的最具启发性的服装。露西·沃斯利（Lucy Worsley）1973年出生于雷丁，是一位历史学家兼电视节目主持人。她在牛津大学获得历史学一等学位，随后在萨塞克斯大学获得艺术史博士学位……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "露西·沃斯利（Lucy Worsley）1973年出生于雷丁，是一位历史学家兼电视节目主持人。她在牛津大学获得历史学一等学位，随后在萨塞克斯大学获得艺术史博士学位。沃斯利曾在历史皇家宫殿担任了21年首席策展人，主管伦敦塔、汉普顿宫和肯辛顿宫等地。她主持了众多纪录片系列，包括《六位王后》、《王室历史上的最大谎言》以及最近的《维多利亚谋杀俱乐部》。她与丈夫住在伦敦。她的最新著作《女王与国王：一段不同寻常的个人历史》现已出版。", "links": [{"text": "Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History", "url": "https://guardianbookshop.com/queens-and-kings-9781399748407/?utm_source=editoriallink&utm_medium=merch&utm_campaign=article"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这是我4岁时的照片。我当时的人生志向是成为一名女巫。我的备选方案是间谍和修女。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们当时住在加拿大。我父亲是寒冷地区——冰川和永久冻土——的专家，他当时正开始与渥太华大学的一位学者进行为期一年的交换项目。我母亲给我做了这套服装，让我和马路对面的家人一起去挨家挨户讨糖果。我的篮子里装满了糖果，我看起来非常高兴也非常骄傲。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因为父亲工作的缘故，我们经常搬家。我天不擅长交朋友，因为我相当害羞。新学校可能会让人望而生畏，但在阅读书籍时，我总能拥有一个安全空间。每当我问父母我小时候是什么样的人时，他们总是说：“我们不知道，因为你总是拿着书看，不跟我们说话。”但在内心深处，我其实是个暗地里的爱出风头者。在借用别人的衣服、性格或人设时，我会表现得很张扬。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在学校之外，我参加了女童子军，演奏乐器并参演话剧。那里没有人知道我是个拿优等成绩的学生，所以我能够伪装成正常人。但在诺丁汉的公立学校，我无处可藏。我是一个怪异的小书呆子，我的好学以一种我当时缺乏社交技巧去掩饰的方式让我显得与众不同。尽管我很孤独，但我因为自己的政治观点而坚持了下来。例如，学生们准备举办一个“随心穿衣日”，以抗议那些总是不断罢工的老师。我不同意，并认为老师们应该罢工，所以我穿着校服去了——这是一个极其愚蠢的选择，所有人都嘲笑了我。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我一直热爱历史，但父亲作为一名科学家，希望我走一条不同的路。为了取悦他，我在高级水平考试中选择了理科科目。进行到一半时，我妈妈说：“你并不喜欢这样。你需要去做你想做的事，那就是历史。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在大学里，我主修古代史和现代史。那段时期我有点行为出格：熬夜到很晚跟那些和我一模一样的人聊天，组织狂欢游行，在乐队里演奏，划船并参加所有课外活动。直到这3年的最后关头我才开始努力学习，因为我忙着享受美妙的时光。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一看到历史皇家宫殿首席策展人职位的招聘广告，我就想：“这就是我的工作！”这是一场漫长的招聘流程，面试在不同的宫殿进行，有一次我在寻找圣詹姆斯宫的正确入口时急得团团转。一个哨兵站在岗亭里，于是我说：“请告诉我正确的路怎么走。我急需赶到。”他本不被允许跟我说话，但最后他心生怜悯，朝我该去的方向翻了个白眼。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这个职位备受瞩目，人们对从事这项工作的人有着某种期待。从历史上看，这个职位一直由男性担任，而且都是具备一定资历的人——那些对自身掌控力极强的人。相比之下，当时我29岁，身材矮小且脸色苍白。我买了一件长款深色大衣，自以为这能让我看起来很成熟。但我的年轻和缺乏经验最终成为了我的超能力，因为每个人都能看出我做事的方式有所不同。我渐渐意识到，我的权威建立在我与交流对象建立信任关系的基础上，而不是让他们觉得我知道得更多。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的电视生涯始于BBC《北方报道》摄制组来到我当时工作的德比郡博尔索弗城堡拍摄纪录片。我们最终一起度过了一天，我向他们展示了如何讲述这里的故事。那天晚上，我被这段经历带给我的巨大快乐所震撼。我开始作为专家“谈话头”出现在各种节目中，并在2008年制作了一档关于亨利八世的节目。随后有了更多作品。世界在变——我不是西蒙·沙玛（Simon Schama）也不是大卫·斯塔基（David Starkey）——而我们已经准备好让更多女性来讲述历史。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "通讯订阅推广之后", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
Born in Reading in 1973, Lucy Worsley is a historian and TV presenter. She ­graduated with a first in history from Oxford, before completing a PhD in art history at the University of Sussex. Worsley spent 21 years as chief curator of Historic Royal Palaces, overseeing the Tower of London, Hampton Court and Kensington Palace, among others. She has p­resented numerous documentary series, including Six Wives, Royal History’s Biggest Fibs and most recently Victorian Murder Club. She lives in London with her husband. Her latest book, Queens and Kings: An Unusually Personal History , is out now.

This is me at the age of four . It was my career ambition to become a witch. My back-up options were spy and nun.

We were living in Canada at the time. Dad was an expert in cold places – glaciers and permanently frozen ground – and he was embarking on a year’s swap with an academic at the University of Ottawa. My mother made the costume for me to go trick or treating with the family across the road. In my basket are sweets and I look very pleased and very proud.

Because of my father’s job, we moved around a lot. I wasn’t naturally good at making friends, because I’m quite shy. New schools could be intimidating, but I always had a safe space when reading books. Whenever I ask my parents what I was like as a child, they say, “We don’t know, because you were always reading a book and not talking to us.” Deep down, I was a secret showoff. I was flamboyant when adopting somebody else’s clothes or character or persona.

Outside school I had Guides, played musical instruments and acted in plays. Nobody there knew I was an A-grade student, so I was able to pass for normal. But at my state school in Nottingham, I couldn’t hide. I was a weird little nerd, and my studiousness marked me out in a way that I didn’t have the social skills to conceal. Even though I was lonely, I soldiered on because of my political views. For example, the pupils were going to have a “wear what you like” day to protest about the teachers who were always going on strike. I disagreed, and thought the teachers should strike, so I went in my school uniform – a horrendously stupid choice as everybody laughed at me.

I always loved history , but my father, being a scientist, wanted me to take a different path. To please him, I chose science subjects for my A-levels. Halfway through, my mum said, “You’re not enjoying this. You need to do what you want to do, which is history.”

At university, I studied ancient and modern history. It was a period in which I went mildly off the rails: staying up late talking to people who were just like me, organising the rag parade, playing in orchestras, rowing and doing all the extracurricular activities. I didn’t work hard until the very end of my three years, as I was too busy having a lovely time.

As soon as I saw the advert for the role of chief curator at Historic Royal Palaces, I thought, “That’s my job!” It was a lengthy recruitment process, with interviews in different palaces, and at one point I got in a tizzy looking for the right entrance at the palace of St James. A sentry was standing in a box, so I said, “Please tell me where the right way is. I’m desperate.” He wasn’t allowed to talk to me, but in the end he took pity and rolled his eyes in the direction I should go.

The role was high-profile and there was an expectation of what someone doing that job would be like. Historically, it had been done by men, always of a certain seniority – people very much in command of themselves. By comparison, I was 29 years old, small and pale. I had bought a long, dark coat, which I thought made me look grown up. But my youth and inexperience eventually became my superpowers, because everybody could see there was something different about the way I was going to do things. I came to realise that my authority is in building a relationship of trust with the person I’m talking to, not making them think that I know more.

My TV career began when BBC Look North came to make a film about Bolsover Castle in Derbyshire, where I was working. We ended up spending the day together, with me showing them how they could tell the story. That night I was struck by how much I enjoyed the experience. I began appearing as an expert “talking head” on various shows, and in 2008 I did a show about Henry VIII. More followed. The world was changing – I wasn’t Simon Schama or David Starkey – and we were ready for more women to talk about history.

after newsletter promotion

The struggle to look “authoritative” that I’d experienced earlier came up again in my TV career. I would get notes such as, “She needs to wear tailoring. She needs a dark coat.” It felt wrong. I am known for wearing costumes – using whatever it takes to tell a story. Like a primary school teacher, I have no dignity. But that is also the skill that is available to me. The dressing up might be considered frivolous by critics, but clothes tell us about hierarchy and social structures. They are also fun to look at, which is important when making TV.

Each day is different on set, but some are stranger than others. In one of my early shows, I was dressed as a medieval peasant foraging in the woods. My costume was a brown blanket. It was November and really cold, but I didn’t have the confidence to say, “This isn’t working for me.” In the end, I just burst into tears. Crying does work, but it’s better to speak up: I did a programme about the American Revolution once, and said to the producer, “I’d really like to be in the Independence Day procession that goes through Philadelphia on 4 July.” I imagined I’d be in a modest costume with buttons and a hat, maybe playing the cymbals. It turned out I was part of a twirling team and my costume was a skin-tight leotard. The rest of the team were 22-year-old girls. I got changed, but agreed with the cameraman that he would only shoot me from the neck up.

Being recognised is wonderful and terrible, as I’m a showoff but also shy. I’m capable of slipping through the streets of London in my baseball cap and glasses, but one in a thousand people have weirdly impressive facial recognition skills and clock me. Once a lady recognised me from my teeth alone. I also have a distinctive voice. Someone overheard me speaking in a swimming pool and said, “I know that voice!” I thought, “I’m naked, I’m dripping. I don’t want to engage with you just now, but thank you.”

The story of my life has been “the bookworm shall go to the ball”. I’ve had a wonderful career. But since turning 50, I’ve realised I work too hard. I’m endlessly asking myself, “Do you really love your work? Or is it just the capitalist patriarchy that’s making you think you love your work because that’s good for the economy?”

I don’t have the answers. But that’s the job of the historian. To ask the questions – and, for me, to put on the costumes. So has the girl in the photo grown up at all? Perhaps not.

article_text:
Shows

“I Dwell in Possibility” by the Museum of Contemporary Art Ahmedabad and GALLERYSKE

I Dwell in Possibility The Museum of Contemporary Art Ahmedabad & GALLERYSKE Ahmedabad Sep 18–Nov 1, 2026

Live plants are an unusual sight in a gallery, yet they populate “I Dwell in Possibility,” sharing the floor with the art as equals. From birds of paradise to bundled palm leaves, these botanical interventions by landscape architect Aditya Shah bring ecology indoors, softening the corporate office space that is currently the satellite venue of the Museum of Contemporary Art Ahmedabad (MCAA). Founded by Indian art collector Aneri D. Patel, the institution marks the first of its kind in the city, set to open its flagship location in the coming years.

“I Dwell in Possibility” is MCAA’s inaugural exhibition, organized in collaboration with GALLERYSKE and gathering works by Avinash Veeraraghavan, Buddhadev Mukherjee, Dia Mehhta Bhupal, Sudarshan Shetty, and Sunil Padwal. The show reads as a primer for the museum’s vision, deriving its title from the opening line of Emily Dickinson’s 19th-century poem, which metaphorizes the boundless creativity of poetry through the motif of a house. Here, each artwork is framed as a window into another discipline, and the exhibition emphasizes the viewers’ comfort through homely and interactive elements: one can sit on the furniture, drawn from Phantom Hands’s Geoffrey Bawa Collection; pick up a book, selected by economist Arjun Jayadev to accompany each artwork; peruse the various recipes supplied by culinary researcher Sheetal Bhatt; or listen to a soundtrack, put together by music archivist Nishant Mittal, through wireless headsets.

Installation views of “I Dwell in Possibility” at the Museum of Contemporary Art Ahmedabad (MCAA), Ahmedabad, 2026. Courtesy MCAA and GALLERYSKE, New Delhi/Bangalore.

Interiority runs through the exhibition, with each artist offering a unique reading of inner worlds and lived spaces. Avinash Veeraraghavan’s Blind Visionary (2024) limns surreal mindscapes in embroidery and video. Buddhadev Mukherjee’s watercolors on silk, Living Together in Fragments (2026), locate the self in daily rituals, with humor as the hinge. Dia Mehhta Bhupal’s prints depict life-size sets of public and private spaces—from movie theaters to locker rooms—constructed by the artist herself from hand-rolled magazine paper. Sudarshan Shetty’s No Title (2013) comprises a wooden frame with acrylic letters spelling out “sometimes when we travel we forget who we are,” considering how objects carry memory and impermanence.

Sunil Padwal’s Overlooked Mangroves on Found Paper (2020) is where the show’s premise feels most earned. He sources old documents, banknotes, posters, and archival documents from the Chor Bazaar in Mumbai, and collages them into cartographic portraits of the city, blending past and present. Each fragment arrives with a history of its own; rewarding those who slow down to observe.

This exhibition is an intimate, contemporary ode to Ahmedabad, embodying the city’s culture of hospitality. MCAA’s partnership with the commercial GALLERYSKE, whose program is rooted in collaboration, builds on this communal energy. Odes of this kind tend to affirm more than they challenge, and this one speaks a language that is familiar to the city. What remains to be seen is what the museum will say once it has walls of its own.

Shreya Ajmani is a writer and art professional focusing on art from Asia and its diasporas.
